questions.title: Which European country will announce plans to shut down its only nuclear power plant because of drought-related cooling-water shortages by August 2, 2026?
questions.background: Nuclear power plants that use river water for cooling can face operational restrictions when drought reduces the available water supply.
questions.resolution_criteria: Source of Truth : Official government statements or contemporaneous reporting by established news organizations. Resolution Rule : Identify the European country whose government announces, between July 1 and August 2, 2026, inclusive, plans for a complete shutdown of its sole operating nuclear power plant because drought has reduced the river water available for reactor cooling. The announcement of the shutdown plan is sufficient; the shutdown itself need not have occurred. A partial reduction in electricity output alone does not qualify. Accepted Answer Format : The country's commonly used English name.
questions.current_reasoning: Major factual updates across all top single-plant European river-cooled nuclear operators as WHO warns July 7 of a new severe European heatwave following Western Europe's hottest June on record. First, Krsko NPP's official July 6 statement (nek.si) corrects our prior assumption: Krsko has run continuously at 100% reactor power since its 2025 outage—never breaching its 28C Sava River limit during the June Omega heatwave thanks to its auxiliary cooling towers—though Slovenia remains #1 (0.48 -> 0.34) because its sole single-reactor plant sits on the small Sava River (25 m3/s flow demand) and NEK noted expert discussions on preparing for recurring extremes. Second, Nuclearelectrica confirmed July 1 (dcbusiness.ro) that Cernavoda Unit 1 is offline in a planned outage leaving ONLY Unit 2 running at Romania's sole nuclear plant (Danube already at 26C); combined with Cernavoda's unique August 2003 complete drought-shutdown precedent on low Danube levels, Romania jumps sharply (0.16 -> 0.30). Third, Hungary's Paks (4 reactors) received a ministerial thermal-limit exemption (30C -> 31.5C) on June 29-30 to avoid deep cuts and began restoring output July 7 (seeenergy.news), trimming Hungary (0.22 -> 0.19) despite low Danube water levels causing tap-water shortages near Budapest on July 1. Bulgaria (Kozloduy, 2 Danube-cooled reactors) rises (0.09 -> 0.13) on lower-Danube drought exposure, with Belarus at 0.02 (sum 0.98).
